transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-10-16
Start time: 15:30 PDT
Duration: ~62 minutes (recorded)
Attendees: Sophie Patel (Redwood AE), Daniel Kim (Redwood SE), Maya Torres (Aerolith MLOps), Ravi Shah (Aerolith Platform), Lena Ortiz (CTO), Jon Perez (Data Scientist)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be rough):
- Goal: scope POC to validate inference economics and tail latency for Aerolith's real-time summarization + search assistant product.
- Key inputs requested: 14 days anonymized logs, token length distributions, SLA targets for 95/99 pct, and top-heavy QPS periods.
- Success criteria: 95th < 120ms for single-turn queries at 40 qps 95% of daytime, 99th < 350ms for peak with fallback; cost target <$0.002 per user request (approx).

Topics: workload shape, QPS/concurrency, input/output token distribution, benchmark harness, POC timeline, security considerations

Transcript body:
[00:00] Sophie (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Sophie from Redwood, and with me is Daniel, our solutions engineer. How's everyone doing?
[00:06] Maya (Aerolith): Hey Sophie, good thanks. Busy but good. Thanks for fitting us in.
[00:09] Daniel (SE): Morning, all. I saw the notes — we'll try to keep this tight and get the scoping to a checklist.
[00:14] Ravi (Platform): Thanks — we want to make sure we give you the right traffic so you can size the POC correctly.
[00:18] Sophie: Great. Quick agenda: one, understand current production traffic and 95/99 latency expectations; two, map QPS and concurrency; three, walk through token distributions (input/out); four, agree success criteria and milestones.
[00:28] Lena (CTO): Sounds good. We're most concerned about tail latency and cost per request.
[00:31] Jon (Data Scientist): Also, some of our requests have large context — long documents for summarization — so token mix is skewed.
[00:37] Daniel: Perfect, that informs batching and KV-cache behavior. Can you give us a rough split of request types? Short questions vs long summarization vs rerank?
[00:44] Maya: Roughly 60% short queries (search assistant), 30% document summarizes (avg 1,200 input tokens, output 200 tokens), 10% rerank/embedding flows.
[00:54] Sophie: Helpful. And what's your 95/99 latency SLO today?
[00:58] Ravi: For interactive search we aim for 95th under 120ms, 99th under 350ms. For summarization flows we accept higher; 95th about 500ms, 99th around 1.2s.
[01:08] Daniel: Good. For the POC we should align a narrower success criteria so we can measure. Proposed: validate that for the interactive mix at daytime QPS of 40 sustained, 95th < 120ms on Redwood Dedicated profile, and cost per request in target band. Thoughts?
[01:23] Lena: 40 qps sounds about right for peak for one cluster — but our peaks are bursty, like short spikes to 180 qps for 30–90 seconds.
[01:33] Sophie: Noted. We'll need burst modeling. Daniel, do you want to explain how we model burst capacity and token mix?
[01:38] Daniel: Sure. We normally create a synthetic load shape: baseline QPS, periodic bursts with poisson arrivals layered to approximate spikiness, and per-request token distributions sampled from your logs. For summarization you get long token sequences that blow up compute; for short queries it's mostly generation tokens that are small. For tail latency we emphasize worst-case sequences for KV cache cold starts.
[01:58] Jon: Our logs show 82% of sessions are short (<300 input tokens), but 1.6% are over 2k tokens and they disproportionately increase 99th latencies.
[02:08] Daniel: That's typical. For POC we can run two benchmark scenarios: (A) production-mix replay (sampled from logs) and (B) adversarial heavy-tail runs focusing on long-context summaries. The replay validates economic unit cost; the adversarial shows tail behavior and fallback policies.
[02:24] Maya: How much data do you need from us for a faithful replay?
[02:27] Daniel: About 10–14 days of anonymized request records with fields: request timestamp, estimated input token count, estimated output token count, route/type. If you can also tag which requests hit cacheable prefixes that helps.
[02:40] Maya: We can do that. We'll sanitize IDs and remove PII.
[02:45] Sophie: Excellent. For concurrency mapping — we ask for per-second QPS distribution or a heatmap of concurrency over time. Ravi, do you have a rough idea of concurrent open connections?
[02:56] Ravi: Our frontend holds requests for ~1.2s on average for short queries, so concurrency is roughly QPS * avg latency. We see average QPS of 12 outside of peak, concurrency around 15; at peak 40 qps sustained concurrency ~50, and during microbursts concurrency hits 200.
[03:13] Daniel: That helps. We'll translate that into the number of simultaneous model workers required using Redwood's batching curves. For short queries, batching helps but at the cost of added queuing latency — we tune batch windows to stay within SLO.
[03:27] Jon: Is there an opportunity to use prefix caching to reduce repeated tokens? Our search assistant often repeats a user prompt template with small differences.
[03:34] Daniel: Yes — prefix/KV caching can reduce token compute for repeated prompts. If you can mark template prefixes in the logs we can model cache hit ratio. Even 20–30% hits on the prompt prefix can materially lower cost and tail latency.
[03:47] Maya: We'll try to annotate.
[03:49] Lena: About security — we may need VPC/private deployment for compliance in Q2. Would that change capacity or latency?
[03:58] Sophie: The private option can add a small network egress overhead depending on where it's hosted but the runtime is identical. For POC we'll do hosted Dedicated to iterate fast; we can replicate to private later with sizing adjustments.
[04:11] Ravi: Ok makes sense. For the benchmarks, what's your harness? Do you run streaming vs non-streaming?
[04:16] Daniel: We have a benchmark harness that supports both. For streaming responses we'll measure time-to-first-token and time-to-last-token. For non-streaming we measure total completion latency. For cost we log tokenization and per-token compute to estimate per-request cost.
[04:30] Sophie: Quick question on metrics — what KPI will you use to decide POC success?
[04:33] Maya: Three main things: 1) Tail latency meeting our SLOs for interactive flows, 2) Cost per request for production-mix under threshold, 3) No functional regressions in output quality.
[04:44] Daniel: For quality we'll do a small eval set — say 200 golden queries across different types, we'll run before/after/per model and check divergence. Can you provide those?
[04:53] Jon: Yes we have an eval set — I'll extract 200 examples across categories and annotate acceptable tolerances.
[04:58] Sophie: Great. On timeline — proposed POC window: 2 weeks of setup + 3 days baseline replay + 2 days adversarial runs + 1 week analysis = roughly 4 weeks total. Does that align?
[05:10] Lena: That's reasonable; can we aim to start benching week of 10/27?
[05:14] Sophie: We can do that if we receive logs by 10/20 and Redwood provides a small infra prep by 10/23.
[05:20] Daniel: Also we'll provision a dedicated GPU pool for the POC with autoscale for bursts. We'll need to agree on a cap so we don't overrun cost. We'll propose a cap of 3x baseline for microbursts.
[05:31] Ravi: Sounds fine. How will you simulate burst traffic exactly? Poisson? Something with heavy tails?
[05:36] Daniel: We typically use a mixture: gamma distribution for baseline variability plus occasional Pareto bursts to mimic heavy-tailed events. We calibrate parameters to match your observed percentiles.
[05:47] Maya: If we give you percentiles (p50/p95/p99) per hour, is that enough?
[05:51] Daniel: It's a good start, but per-second resolution for a couple of peak days helps tune microburst duration. Otherwise we might under or over provision for tail behavior.
[05:59] Jon: One more nuance: for long summarization requests we sometimes precompute embeddings and then run a generation over a subset of the doc. That means some requests look cheap but have upstream costs.
[06:10] Daniel: We'll account for upstream embedding calls as separate cost units in the model; we'll need counts and average cost or we can model with Redwood embeddings metrics if you provide counts.
[06:20] Sophie: Let's talk about success numbers concretely. Proposed POC acceptance: (1) Production-mix replay shows average cost per user request <$0.0025 and 95th latency <= 120ms for interactive flows, (2) adversarial runs show 99th latency no worse than 1.5x current baseline with documented fallback plan, (3) quality regression < 3% on eval set.
[06:41] Lena: The cost target is tough but plausible. We might relax to <$0.003 if caching yields lower overall spend.
[06:49] Maya: Also, what about warm vs cold KV cache? Our real traffic has a warm cache for about 70% of repeated prompts.
[06:57] Daniel: We'll run both warm and cold scenarios: warm hit ratio modeled at your reported 70%, and cold start runs to measure worst-case.
[07:05] Sophie: On reporting — we'll give a spreadsheet with per-scenario metrics: P50/P95/P99 latencies, tokens per request, cost per request, throughput achieved, and recommended quant/scale settings.
[07:15] Jon: Can you recommend quantization levels? We currently use bfloat16 in-house but would consider int8 for inference.
[07:22] Daniel: We'll include recommendations. For long-context models int8 can significantly reduce memory; for latency it depends on kernel support. We'll run a small comparison in the POC.
[07:31] Ravi: About dataset privacy — we need to ensure logs are processed in a way that PII is removed. Is there a preferred schema?
[07:39] Sophie: We can share a minimal schema with fields we need; you can run local transforms and send a sanitized file via S3 presigned URL or secure upload. We'll not request raw payloads, just token counts and timestamps and a sample of prompts if you can sanitize them.
[07:53] Maya: We'll do that.
[07:55] Daniel: Ok, quick run-through of deliverables: Redwood provides benchmark harness repo link, initial traffic model spreadsheet, and POC environment details. Aerolith provides logs, eval set, and target SLOs.
[08:06] Sophie: Are there any blockers from your side?
[08:09] Lena: Only internal approvals for sending logs — security signoff expected by 10/18.
[08:15] Sophie: Great. We'll aim to have the infra prep and pricing sent by 10/18 so we can start the week of 10/27.
[08:22] Jon: One detail — for the adversarial runs, can you throttle to mimic real network jitter? We care about network impact on streaming TTF.
[08:30] Daniel: Yes, the harness can add jitter, packet latency emulation, and vary chunk sizes for streaming. We'll include that in the test plan.
[08:39] Maya: Another ask — can you include a cost sensitivity table showing how batching windows change latency/cost tradeoffs?
[08:45] Daniel: Absolutely — we'll model batching latency curves at several window sizes and supply recommendations.
[08:51] Sophie: Anything else from Aerolith?
[08:54] Ravi: Not from me.
[08:55] Lena: No.
[08:56] Sophie: Great. We'll follow up with a short summary and the spreadsheet. Thanks all.

Recap / Agreed next steps (verbatim in call):
- Aerolith to provide 14 days of anonymized logs and 200-eval queries by 2025-10-20.
- Redwood to share benchmark harness, initial traffic model spreadsheet, and pilot pricing by 2025-10-18.
- Schedule benchmark kickoff (60m) for week of 2025-10-27 once logs are in.

End of transcript.
